articles.title: Youth advocates gather in New York to launch new AI standards
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly transforms everything from how we learn, to the job market, children are adopting the technology more than three times faster than adults – exposing them to unique opportunities and risks.
articles.content:
The UN hosted more than 600 young people from around the world on Wednesday at New York Headquarters to discuss how AI can support the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

The summit took place on International Youth Day, which has taken place every 12 August since the year 2000 to celebrate the potential of youth as partners in today’s global society.

Following various discussions and workshops organized by the International Organization of Youth, delegates presented a Youth-led Declaration on AI Policy and Governance. It will inform future UN-led efforts to shape global AI governance, especially the Global Digital Compact.

Tweet URL

The event builds on previous UN efforts to integrate youth voices into decision making processes on AI, including the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Secretary-General’s Youth Advisory Board and the Science, Technology and Innovation Forum.

Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs Felipe Paullier said it was the generation represented in the room who will live longest with the consequences of AI, adding that Youth Day represents an opportunity to listen to young people from different backgrounds on how AI can better serve the future of humanity.

“Young people are sometimes included in these conversations, but they’re actually included only at a few moments,” Mr. Paullier said. “Meaningful youth participation is not about being consulted in a tokenistic way at the end of a process. It’s about involving them at the beginning.”

Underrepresented voices

Samara Allen, a 19-year-old student at the University of California-Los Angeles, moderated the opening session – reflecting the role of young people in leading discussions around AI.

Several ambassadors and UN officials highlighted the fact that because young people will live the longest with the impacts, they must play a role in shaping the future of AI standards across the globe.

“This is not simply a conversation about technology,” Ambassador of Dominica Philbert Aaron said. “It is a conversation about power, dignity, opportunity, culture and the future we choose to build together.”

But young people were not the only marginalised group that representatives at the summit seek to empower.

With ambassadors from the Bahamas and Dominica helping to organise the summit – and with participation from Pakistan and Tonga – delegates also discussed how to ensure that developing countries are not left behind in the AI transition.

“Technological progress will not automatically translate into human progress if developing countries lack access to the infrastructure, computing capacity, skills, finance and knowledge,” said Sheikh Jaffar Khan Mandokhail, governor of the Balochistan region of Pakistan.

Mr. Paullier said it was “unfortunate” that AI development is controlled primarily by a few large companies based in higher-income countries, and stressed that AI governance must be inclusive.

“We want AI to help to reduce inequalities, not to deepen inequalities,” he said.

In a statement on Wednesday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the international day celebrates “the creativity, dynamism and leadership of young people everywhere.”

He recognised that young people face myriad challenges including economic uncertainty, digital inclusion and climate change, and stressed that the UN stands with them as they seek a greater role in decision-making processes.

Young and jobless

Ahead of the day, the UN’s International Labour Organization (ILO) published a report finding that worldwide youth unemployment is beginning to worsen again after a post-pandemic rebound, leaving millions unable to get their crucial first job.

The report further found that 6.1 per cent of jobs currently held by young people aged 15 to 29 fall in the categories of those most exposed to AI, which could lead to millions more becoming unemployed within the next few years.

Speakers said the youth participants at the summit are some of the best positioned to ensure that AI empowers humanity and helps people learn new skills – rather than simply taking jobs.

“The future of AI should not simply happen to your generation. Your generation must actually help shape it,” Mr. Mandokhail said. “My message to you is therefore simple: Learn, question, innovate and lead to build fairer societies, stronger communities and a more sustainable world.”

articles.personality_title: Young leaders unite at UN to shape fair AI future
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing many parts of life, from schools to jobs. Young people are learning and using AI much faster than adults, which brings both new chances and challenges.

**What happened** – On August 12, International Youth Day, over 600 young people from around the world met at the United Nations headquarters in New York. They talked about how AI can help reach global goals for a better future. The event included workshops and discussions led by youth groups and ended with a Youth-led Declaration on AI Policy and Governance. This declaration will help guide future UN decisions about AI.

**Impact** – This gathering is special because it puts young people at the center of important talks about AI, not just as listeners but as leaders. The event also focused on making sure poorer countries and other often overlooked groups have a say in how AI is used worldwide. Experts pointed out that AI should reduce unfairness, not increase it, and that young people will live longest with the effects of these decisions.

**What's next step** – The ideas and declaration from this summit will influence the UN’s Global Digital Compact, a plan to manage AI worldwide. Young people will continue to be included early in decision-making. Countries and organizations will work to make AI safer and fairer for everyone, especially in places that might otherwise be left behind.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Young people from around the world are leading the way to create AI rules that are fair, inclusive, and designed to help all communities thrive.

articles.title: A strange crystal made of electrons just revealed its hidden motion
articles.summary: Physicists have found a new way to peer inside one of matter’s most elusive quantum states: the Wigner crystal, where electrons stop behaving like independent particles and organize into a crystal-like pattern. By shining light on an atomically thin material cooled close to absolute zero, researchers uncovered optical signals that reveal not just where the electrons are, but how they move together.
articles.content:
Researchers at the University of Basel and the Technical University of Munich have found a new way to examine how electrons move together inside one of the most elusive forms of matter, the Wigner crystal. By using light to probe this delicate quantum state, the physicists uncovered properties that had previously been extremely difficult to observe.

When electrons are restricted to a two-dimensional plane and interact strongly enough, they can begin behaving very differently from ordinary electrons. Instead of moving independently, they arrange themselves into a repeating pattern similar to the orderly structure of atoms in a conventional crystal.

This unusual arrangement is called a Wigner crystal. Scientists have studied it for decades because the crystal structure is created by interactions between the electrons themselves rather than by the underlying structure of the material containing them.

While researchers have already detected Wigner crystals in a variety of physical systems, understanding what happens inside them has been much harder. Scientists have struggled to directly investigate how their electrons move collectively, interact with one another, and react to outside disturbances.

Using Light to Probe a Wigner Crystal

In a study published in Nature Physics, experimental researchers led by Professor Tomasz Smoleński at the University of Basel examined a single atomic layer of tungsten diselenide that had been cooled to only a few degrees above absolute zero.

The team illuminated the material and carefully analyzed the light reflected from it. Those measurements revealed previously unseen optical features that contain information about the collective behavior of electrons inside the Wigner crystal.

The signals emerge from interactions between the ordered electrons and excitations created in the material by light, known as excitons. Together, these components form hybrid quasiparticles called Wigner crystal polarons. These quasiparticles serve as highly sensitive optical probes that can reveal both the crystal itself and the collective motion occurring within it.

"Our measurements show that light can do more than simply detect the presence of this exotic state -- it can reveal how the state behaves internally," says first author Dr. Lujun Wang from the University of Basel, who carried out the experiments together with Ferdinand Menzel, a PhD student in Smoleński's group.

"This gives us a powerful new tool for studying collective excitations of electronic crystals that would otherwise be extremely difficult to access," adds Smoleński.

Electron Interactions Shape the Optical Signals

The researchers also discovered that the strength of the interactions between electrons influences the optical signatures they observed. That connection could make the signals especially useful for investigating strongly correlated systems, where the behavior of the material emerges from interactions among many particles rather than from individual particles acting on their own.

To account for the experimental findings, a theoretical team led by Professor Michael Knap at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) developed a model describing the formation of Wigner crystal polarons. Their work explains how these quasiparticles arise through the coupling of optically generated excitons with the collective movement of electrons in the crystal.

A New View of Strongly Correlated Quantum Matter

"What is particularly exciting is that these signals carry information not only about how the electrons are arranged, but also about their quantum dynamics," explains Fabian Pichler, a PhD student at TUM. "This allows us to connect the experimental observations directly to the underlying many-body physics."

The findings suggest that atomically thin materials could provide an especially useful platform for observing how electrons move collectively within ordered quantum states. By making these hidden dynamics easier to study, the approach could help scientists develop a deeper understanding of strongly correlated matter and the complex behavior that emerges when many particles interact.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in understanding the elusive Wigner crystal quantum state by developing a novel optical probing method. This discovery provides a powerful new tool to study collective electron behavior in strongly correlated quantum matter, which has broad implications for quantum physics and materials science. The research is detailed, focused, and represents a meaningful advance with potential wide-ranging benefits for science and technology.

articles.title: Mammal ancestors were giving birth to live young 236 million years ago
articles.summary: Almost all mammals give birth rather than laying eggs, and we have new clues about when they began to do so
articles.content:
Almost all mammals give birth rather than laying eggs, and we have new clues about when they began to do so

A reconstruction of a group of Chiniquodon theotonicus María de los Ángeles Miceli Baro

Creatures that bridged the gap between reptiles and mammals may have been bearing live young 90 million years earlier than we thought.

One of the hallmarks of all mammals apart from monotremes – echidnas and the platypus – is that they give birth to live young. This “viviparity” contrasts with the “oviparity” seen most other vertebrates, in which females lay eggs that hatch outside their bodies.

One long-standing question has been whether creatures known as cynodonts, which emerged around 260 million years ago during the Permian geological period and are directly ancestral to all mammals, laid eggs or gave birth to live young, as no evidence of their reproduction has been discovered either way.

Advertisement

“Whether mammalian ancestors were oviparous or viviparous has been considered a mystery,” says Leandro Gaetano at Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council. “We had no clues on how or when one of the most distinctive traits of the majority of present-day mammals, viviparity, evolved in the mammalian lineage.”

This has now changed, thanks to a chance observation made during a postgraduate class at the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina. The students were examining a fossil of Chiniquodon theotonicus, a cynodont that lived 236 million years ago and was unearthed in the Talampaya National Park in north-western Argentina in 2011. Part of the analysis involved using a microscope to examine thin slices taken from one of the ancient animal’s leg bones. At that point, the class noticed a curious growth line inside the bone.

Gaetano and his colleagues investigated further and eventually concluded that this line, analogous to a tree’s growth ring, recorded the moment that the ancient mammal relative went through a growth spurt after its birth.

The researchers reconstructed how large the leg bone and the animal itself would have been when the growth line formed. They calculated that the animal would have weighed 1.68 kilograms at that point. When the animal died as a full-grown adult, it was just shy of 12 kilograms.

This gave the researchers a ratio of newborn to adult size in the ancient animal. They then compared this figure to similar ratios obtained from a wide variety of modern animals: 1869 mammals, 2619 non-avian reptiles and 782 birds.

“We were amazed to find that Chiniquodon grouped with extant placental mammals,” says Gaetano.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter

Egg-laying animal groups produce young that are far smaller than adults when they hatch, he says.

For example, some species of large birds have newly hatched young that are just 0.002 per cent of adult body mass, whereas placental mammals often give birth to young that are over 20 per cent of the size of their parents.

“Only placental mammals produce relatively large newborns, whereas reptile and bird hatchlings are comparatively very small,” says Gaetano. “Hence, we propose that [the] Chiniquodon theotonicus reproductive strategy was most similar to that of placental mammals.”

Mike Benton at the University of Bristol in the UK says the findings are convincing.

“Further, as they argue, the apparent absence or rarity of actual eggs of any kind in the Permian and Triassic has always been puzzling – the so-called amniote egg gap,” he says.

Oliver Griffith at Macquarie University in Sydney says his gut reaction is to be sceptical of the claim of live birth, as we have only indirect evidence. But he is impressed that, in the absence of any direct fossil evidence, the team is still trying to solve the puzzle.

“We may never get any of the kind of direct evidence that solves the

mystery, for example a fossilised mammalian egg or a fossil mother during

pregnancy,” he says. “So it is kind of cool that they’re taking a different approach to trying to find an answer to that question.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that mammal ancestors gave birth to live young 236 million years ago, pushing back the timeline for viviparity in mammalian lineage by 90 million years. This breakthrough enhances understanding of evolutionary biology with broad significance for science and society.
articles.personality_title: Scientists find mammal ancestors gave birth to live young 236 million years ago
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Most mammals today give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs. Scientists have long wondered when this change first happened in the ancestors of mammals, called cynodonts, which lived hundreds of millions of years ago.

**What happened** – A team of researchers in Argentina studied a fossil of Chiniquodon theotonicus, a cynodont from 236 million years ago. They looked closely at growth lines inside the animal’s leg bone and discovered signs that the baby grew inside the mother, similar to how modern mammals grow.

**Impact** – This finding suggests that mammal ancestors were giving birth to live young about 90 million years earlier than scientists thought. It helps explain a big mystery about how mammals evolved and shows that giving birth to live babies started much earlier than expected. The study compared the size of the newborn animal to adults and found it matched modern placental mammals, which have relatively large babies.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to study fossils and use new methods to learn more about how early mammals lived and reproduced. This discovery encourages researchers to look for more indirect evidence to understand ancient animals better since direct proof like fossilized eggs or pregnant mothers is very rare.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New research shows mammal ancestors were giving birth to live young 236 million years ago, pushing back the start of this key mammal trait by 90 million years.

articles.title: Agentic profiles for effective AI governance
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10805-zA framework comprising four dimensions—autonomy, efficacy, goal complexity and generality—is proposed for characterizing AI agents, supporting the construction of agentic profiles for the effective governance of different AI agents.

Feigenbaum, E. A. The art of artificial intelligence: themes and case studies of knowledge engineering. In Proc. 5th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI ’77) Vol. 2, 1014–1029 (Morgan Kaufmann, 1977).

articles.personality_title: New framework helps guide safer and smarter AI systems
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more powerful and widespread, experts are looking for ways to manage and control these systems to keep them safe and useful. AI agents are programs that can make decisions and act on their own, but not all AI agents are the same. Understanding their differences is important for good rules and oversight.

**What happened** – Researchers have created a new framework to describe AI agents using four key features: autonomy (how independently they act), efficacy (how well they achieve goals), goal complexity (how complicated their tasks are), and generality (how many different tasks they can handle). This helps build detailed 'agentic profiles' that explain how an AI agent works and what risks it might have. The framework was published online in August 2026 in the journal Nature.

**Impact** – This framework is important because it gives governments, companies, and researchers a clearer way to understand and govern AI agents. By knowing these four dimensions, they can create better rules to ensure AI behaves safely and ethically. It also helps address challenges like AI making complex decisions without human oversight or acting unpredictably. This approach supports safer AI development and use across many areas like healthcare, business, and public services.

**What's next step** – The next step is for policymakers and AI developers to use this framework when designing AI systems and laws. Researchers will also test and improve these agentic profiles to cover more types of AI agents. Over time, this could lead to international standards that help everyone understand and control AI technology effectively.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new four-part framework offers a clear way to describe and govern AI agents, helping ensure they are safe and reliable as their role in society grows.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau cadre pour mieux encadrer les systèmes d’IA en toute sécurité
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Avec le développement rapide de l’intelligence artificielle (IA), il est essentiel de trouver des moyens pour la gérer et la contrôler afin qu’elle reste sûre et utile. Les agents d’IA sont des programmes capables de prendre des décisions seuls, mais ils sont très différents les uns des autres. Comprendre ces différences est important pour établir de bonnes règles.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont proposé un nouveau cadre pour décrire les agents d’IA selon quatre caractéristiques principales : autonomie (leur indépendance), efficacité (leur capacité à atteindre des objectifs), complexité des buts (la difficulté des tâches) et généralité (leur capacité à gérer plusieurs tâches). Ce cadre permet de créer des « profils agentiques » détaillés qui expliquent comment un agent fonctionne et quels risques il peut présenter. Cette étude a été publiée en août 2026 dans la revue Nature.

**Impact** – Ce cadre est important car il offre aux gouvernements, entreprises et chercheurs un moyen clair de comprendre et de réguler les agents d’IA. En connaissant ces quatre dimensions, ils peuvent établir de meilleures règles pour garantir un comportement sûr et éthique de l’IA. Cela aide aussi à gérer les défis liés aux décisions complexes prises par l’IA sans supervision humaine. Cette approche favorise un développement et une utilisation plus sûrs de l’IA dans des secteurs comme la santé, les affaires ou les services publics.

**Prochaine étape** – Il s’agit maintenant pour les décideurs et développeurs d’intégrer ce cadre dans la conception des systèmes d’IA et des lois. Les chercheurs continueront à tester et améliorer ces profils pour couvrir plus de types d’agents. À terme, cela pourrait conduire à des normes internationales pour mieux comprendre et contrôler la technologie de l’IA.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Un nouveau cadre en quatre parties permet de décrire clairement et de mieux réguler les agents d’IA, assurant leur sécurité et fiabilité à mesure qu’ils prennent de l’importance dans la société.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo marco para guiar sistemas de IA más seguros y eficientes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – A medida que la inteligencia artificial (IA) se vuelve más poderosa y común, los expertos buscan formas de gestionarla para que sea segura y útil. Los agentes de IA son programas que pueden tomar decisiones por sí mismos, pero no todos son iguales. Entender sus diferencias es clave para crear buenas reglas y supervisión.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores han creado un nuevo marco para describir a los agentes de IA usando cuatro características principales: autonomía (qué tan independientes actúan), eficacia (qué tan bien logran sus objetivos), complejidad de metas (qué tan complicadas son sus tareas) y generalidad (cuántas tareas diferentes pueden realizar). Esto ayuda a construir «perfiles agenticos» detallados que explican cómo funciona un agente y qué riesgos puede tener. El marco fue publicado en agosto de 2026 en la revista Nature.

**Impacto** – Este marco es importante porque ofrece a gobiernos, empresas e investigadores una forma clara de entender y gobernar a los agentes de IA. Al conocer estas cuatro dimensiones, pueden crear mejores reglas para asegurar que la IA actúe de forma segura y ética. También ayuda a enfrentar desafíos como la toma de decisiones complejas sin supervisión humana. Este enfoque apoya un desarrollo y uso más seguros de la IA en áreas como salud, negocios y servicios públicos.

**Próximo paso** – El siguiente paso es que los responsables de políticas y desarrolladores usen este marco al diseñar sistemas y leyes de IA. Los investigadores también probarán y mejorarán estos perfiles para cubrir más tipos de agentes. Con el tiempo, esto podría llevar a estándares internacionales para entender y controlar mejor la tecnología de IA.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Un nuevo marco de cuatro partes ofrece una forma clara de describir y gobernar agentes de IA, ayudando a garantizar que sean seguros y confiables a medida que su papel en la sociedad crece.
